summary: Vitales - Crew Health Check is health software for a crew that Earth can't help in time. On Mars a message to mission control takes 4 to 24 minutes each way, and NASA's exploration medicine team plans for "No evacuations possible". It runs offline on one laptop and its webcam. Using NASA's Clinical Findings Forms, it checks each of the 119 conditions NASA models for exploration missions against the kit on board, then marks on the crew member's body what this ship can measure and what it has no test for. With a station kit, 9 conditions get a measurement, 82 depend on what the person reports, and 28 need a test that isn't aboard. Every condition has a plan the crew can follow with the ground link down and the AI switched off. When the medical officer is the patient, a crewmate without medical training learns to take a pulse by hand, and the hub accepts the count only when the camera agrees. A potency engine estimates how much of each stored medicine still works. An optional local medical model explains the plans but can't change a warning. The same map tells a mission what to pack and whom to train.
details:
What it does

Vitales - Crew Health Check answers two questions for a crew far from Earth: with this kit, can we tell what's wrong, and what do we do about it here?

The kit map has one row for each of the 119 conditions on NASA's exploration condition list. Each row links to that condition's NASA Clinical Findings Form, and the hub checks the form's confirming test against the kit aboard. The crew app draws the answer on the body: a dot where the kit can measure, a ring where only the person's own report is possible, and an open ring where the test that would confirm it isn't aboard. With a station kit (webcam, pulse oximeter, blood pressure cuff, thermometer, wrist band), 9 conditions get a measurement, 82 rely on what the person reports and 28 need a test that isn't aboard. Adding an ultrasound for a Mars mission changes that to 16, 81 and 22.

Every condition also has a plan aboard: 119 plans, plus 20 first-aid flows behind the Someone needs help button. Plans run in stages and end in a stated mode, such as resolve here or stabilize and watch. The log for the ground is always the last step. Where the ship lacks a test, a step stands in for it and says what it can't replace, for example "It cannot replace an ECG".

Teach and check covers the case where the medical officer is the patient or outside on a surface walk. The app walks a crewmate with no medical training through a pulse check one step at a time while they tap each beat. The hub compares their count with the pulse the webcam measures from the face (remote photoplethysmography) and records whether the two agree. If the camera signal is poor, it refuses the reading and says why.

A Mars kit has to outlast its shelf life, so the potency engine follows each medicine lot through its storage history (temperature, humidity, light, radiation dose) and estimates how much active drug is left, when the lot will fall out of specification, and which lot to use first. It never answers a dosing question.

The ground link schedule comes from NASA's lunar and Mars communication documents. Messages for Earth wait in a queue until the next contact, and no plan step waits for a reply.

The AI is optional: a local medical model, HuatuoGPT-3-9B on llama.cpp, that explains plans and asks the next question. Offline on our reference laptop it answered 317 of 400 MedQA questions correctly (79.3%), a benchmark built from the US medical licensing exam. The dataset, weights, runtime and chat template are pinned by SHA-256, so the run can be repeated byte for byte. The model only listens on the laptop itself, its tools have closed schemas, and the rule that it can't change a warning or a plan is enforced in code. Every plan and the emergency flow work with it switched off.

Why it matters

NASA's Integrated Medical Model "assumes that all medical conditions are correctly diagnosed by the crew". Our kit map checks that assumption condition by condition against a real kit. A crew gets decisions packed before launch instead of waiting on a link that may be down for weeks. Mission planners get a list of what a kit can't confirm, which tells them what to pack and whom to train. A remote clinic on Earth with no doctor nearby faces the same two questions.

NASA data

The kit map and plans come from NASA's ExMC condition list and Clinical Findings Forms, the habitat limits from NASA-STD-3001, and the ground link from NASA's lunar and Mars communication documents. The app replays 12 NASA data files (ISS cabin CO2 from OSDR, ISS and Mars surface radiation from RadLab, Increment 71 air and water quality, ISS acoustics, Inspiration4 blood panels) and 7 cases with published outcomes. Each file has a provenance record with its URL and SHA-256. In the replay of the September 2017 solar particle event, the onset detector fires at 04:18:40 UTC on 11 September, inside the ISS pass under way when the event arrived. The full list of over 100 NASA sources is in docs/product/NASA-SOURCES.md.

How we built it

The hub is Python 3.14 with FastAPI and SQLite. The crew app is Vue and TypeScript. The camera worker uses MediaPipe face and pose models. The potency engine uses RDKit and GFN2-xTB quantum chemistry (tblite), with Monte Carlo draws for uncertainty, and an independent implementation written from the spec agrees with it to 1e-9. The hardware is one laptop (our reference is an Apple M3 with 16 GB) and its webcam. The oximeter, cuff, thermometer and habitat sensor are optional: each has a simulated twin that sends the real device's Bluetooth protocol bytes, so the same code runs with or without hardware. Over 4,600 automated tests run on Ubuntu, macOS and Windows.

What we think is new

Health apps usually show what they measure. Ours also shows what the ship can't test and still gives the crew a plan for it. It uses a crewmate's hands as a second sensor and has the camera check them. It also treats the medicine kit as something that degrades over a long mission, and computes by how much.

What we considered

No plan depends on Earth: every plan, help flow and warning runs to the end with the link down. The medical officer can be the patient, which is why teach and check exists. The AI only proposes and deterministic rules decide; it also can't read another crew member's records. Every reading carries a Live, Replay or Sim label and its unit, and missing data stays missing instead of being filled in. We built the project with AI coding tools (Claude Code and Codex) and logged every run in AI-USE-LOG.md. The clinical content was drafted from NASA's forms by one model and checked against them by another.

Limits: Vitales - Crew Health Check is decision support, not a medical device. It hasn't been clinically validated, and its clinical content still needs review by a clinician.
